What actually travels

Your app calls an API and gets JSON back, as if the two were joined by a pipe. Underneath, there's no pipe: only small chunks of data that can get lost. Here's the stack of layers that turns them into a request and a response.

The problem

In your code, a request is one call, and a user object comes back. But the phone and the server are joined by Wi-Fi, a cell tower, cables and a dozen routers, machines that pass data along toward its address, any of which can drop data. How does a request survive that trip, and what does it cost?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Data travels in packets. A small message can fit in one; a large stream spans many. About 1,500 bytes is a common link limit, not a universal packet size.

IP, the Internet Protocol, is the postal service: it addresses each packet and passes it from router to router toward the server. It does its best, nothing more. A packet can be lost, delayed, or overtaken by the one sent after it.

TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, builds something reliable on top. The sender numbers positions in the byte stream. Each segment carries the position of its first byte. An acknowledgement gives the next byte expected; the sender can retransmit missing data, and the receiver delivers bytes in order. Your code sees one clean stream of bytes. To keep that bookkeeping, both sides must first agree to talk: a TCP connection, set up with a short exchange before any data flows.

This diagram follows the stack that uses TCP; other web transports exist. On top of TCP, two more layers:

LayerIts job
HTTPthe request and the response (puzzle 2)
TLSencrypts the stream, so intermediaries cannot read the content or alter it undetected (puzzle 4)
TCPreliable, ordered delivery, over a connection
IPaddresses and routes each packet, best effort

Every puzzle that follows is about the cost of this stack: how long packets take to cross (puzzle 3), what setting up a connection costs (puzzle 5), and what the phone's radio pays to send them (puzzle 6).

The analogy

Sending a book by post, one page per envelope. The post office (IP) delivers most envelopes, in any order, and loses a few. Your friend (TCP) numbers the pages, writes back "got pages 1 to 40", and you resend the missing ones. Before the first page, you agree by letter that you're sending a book at all: the connection.

Check yourself

A packet of your request is lost between two routers. Who notices and fixes it?

Right. Numbering, acknowledging, resending: TCP.

Not quite. Your code sees a clean stream; TCP handles losses underneath.

Not quite. IP only does its best; recovering lost packets is TCP's job.

Why must a TCP connection be set up before the first request?

Not quite. IP delivers every packet anyway; the setup is TCP's bookkeeping.

Right. Reliability needs shared bookkeeping.

Not quite. TLS runs on top of TCP, but the setup is TCP's own need.

What's the difference between IP and TCP?

Right. Best effort vs reliable.

Not quite. That's the two swapped. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • RFC 9293 · Sequence numbers
  • High Performance Browser Networking: Building blocks of TCP ("The IP, or Internet Protocol, is what provides the host-to-host routing and addressing, and TCP, or Transmission Control Protocol, is what provides the abstraction of a reliable network running over an unreliable channel"; TCP hides "retransmission of lost data, in-order delivery, congestion control and avoidance, data integrity")

What you now know

Data crosses the internet in packets. IP addresses each packet and routes it, but can lose, delay or reorder it. TCP turns those packets into a reliable, ordered stream: it numbers bytes, waits for acknowledgements and resends what's lost, and needs a connection set up first. TLS encrypts that stream, and HTTP is the language of requests and responses on top.
